content: Digital Adaptation Kits (DAKs) are primarily designed to ensure the validity and accuracy of health content within digital systems. They provide generic content requirements that are independent of specific software applications, allowing countries to customize them according to local needs. These kits are based on systems that offer functionalities such as digital tracking and decision support (DTDS). Components of DAKs include personas, workflows, core data elements, decision-support algorithms, scheduling logic, and reporting indicators. Practical resources, such as spreadsheets containing data dictionaries and detailed decision-support algorithms, are included to assist implementers in developing digital systems. Additionally, data components within DAKs are mapped to standardized terminologies, such as the International Classification of Diseases (ICD), to facilitate interoperability. DAKs adopt a modular approach to detail the data and content requirements for specific health program areas, such as antenatal care and child health. They align with validated health practices and recommended guidelines to ensure consistency and adherence to clinical and public health standards. The foundational layer of DAKs includes leadership, governance, strategy, investments, legislation, workforce standards, interoperability, and infrastructure. Digital tracking involves the use of digitized records to capture and store clients' health information, enabling follow-up on their health status and services received. This may include electronic patient records linked to uniquely identified individuals. Digital tracking aims to reduce lapses in continuity of care by facilitating timely follow-up contacts and incorporating decision-support tools to guide health workers in executing clinical protocols. It also supports scheduling upcoming services and following checklists for appropriate case management at the point of care. Health worker decision support is defined as digitized job aids that combine an individual’s health information with clinical protocols to assist health workers in making diagnostic and treatment decisions. A person-centered DTDS system includes a persistent record of health events and encounters, linking to clinical decision-support systems to reinforce good practices. It also connects to reporting and management tools to enhance accountability. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends digital targeted client communication for health issues related to sexual, reproductive, maternal, newborn, and child health, provided concerns about sensitive content and data privacy are addressed. WHO also recommends the use of digital decision support accessible via mobile devices for community and facility-based health workers, as long as the tasks are within their defined scope of practice. Digital tracking combined with decision support and targeted client communication is recommended under specific conditions, such as integrated implementation within the health system and adherence to data privacy standards. DAKs are part of a broader strategic vision for SMART guidelines, which aim to maximize health impact through improved fidelity and uptake of recommendations within standards-based digital systems. These guidelines involve a systematic process for transforming guideline development, delivery, and application into machine-readable, adaptive, and testable formats. DAKs serve as a prerequisite for developing computable guidelines and advanced analytics for precision health. The components of a DAK include health interventions and recommendations, generic personas, user scenarios, business processes and workflows, core data elements, decision-support logic, indicators and reporting requirements, and high-level functional and non-functional requirements. Each component provides a generic starting point that can be adapted to specific contexts. For example, decision-support logic includes algorithms to support service delivery in line with WHO guidelines, while indicators and performance metrics are based on data feasibly captured from routine digital systems. DAKs have been developed for various health domains, including antenatal care, family planning, HIV, immunizations, and postnatal care. They aim to standardize software requirements for primary health care settings, ensuring consistency and adherence to global health standards.
